source: Piaget (1936-1970) four-stage theory, as summarised on Wikipedia
finding: Piaget proposed four invariant stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational. Each stage is a new way of organising knowledge, reached by assimilation and accommodation.
numbers: Sensorimotor birth-24 months (6 substages: 0-6w, 6w-4m, 4-8m, 8-12m, 12-18m, 18-24m). Preoperational ~2-7y. Concrete operational 7-11y. Formal operational from 11, final at 14-15.
limits: Secondary source (Wikipedia). Ages are approximate and now seen as task-dependent. Piaget's own books were not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only. Stages are a scaffold for describing capability growth, not a recipe for an LLM.

source: Piaget's theory: object permanence and A-not-B (Wikipedia summary)
finding: Piaget saw object permanence arrive in stages. At 8-12 months infants search for hidden objects but make the A-not-B error. Full understanding comes at 18-24 months. Baillargeon and DeVos found surprise at impossible events in infants as young as 3.5 months.
numbers: Stage 3 (4-8m): reach for partly hidden, not fully hidden objects. Stage 4 (8-12m): A-not-B error. Stage 6 (18-24m): errors stop. Baillargeon & DeVos 1991: car/mouse and carrot events, infants 3.5 months.
limits: The page gives no sample sizes and omits the 1985 study and the dynamic-systems critique.
agent_relevance: Shows that 'passes the test' depends on the response format (reaching vs looking). Same for LLM benchmarks: answer format changes the measured stage.

source: Pascual-Leone, Case, Halford, Fischer, Demetriou: neo-Piagetian theories (Wikipedia summary)
finding: Neo-Piagetians keep Piaget's stages but explain stage change by growth in processing capacity: working memory (Pascual-Leone, Case), relational complexity (Halford), skill levels (Fischer), speed and control (Demetriou).
numbers: Pascual-Leone mental power: ~1 unit at age 2-3, +1 every second year, max 7 at age 15. Case stages: sensorimotor 1-18m, interrelational 18m-5y, dimensional 5-11y, vectorial 11-19y. Halford: unary ~1y, binary ~3y, ternary ~5y, quaternary ~10y. Fischer tiers: representations single ~2y, mappings 3.5-4.5y, systems 6-7y, abstractions 10-12y, 14-16y, 18-20y.
limits: Secondary source. Exact M-power per task is not given there. The ages are group averages and each programme draws its boundaries differently.
agent_relevance: All four programmes share one claim that matters for us: task difficulty scales with how many items or relations must be held and bound at once. That is a testable load knob for prompts.

source: Demetriou et al., speed and working-memory data (via Wikipedia neo-Piagetian page)
finding: Demetriou's data show processing speed and working-memory span both change with age and relate to reasoning level, with peaks of speed-intelligence relation near 2-3, 6-7 and 11-13 years.
numbers: Spatial WM ~3 units at age 6, ~5 at 12. Math WM ~2 at 6, ~4 at 12. WM with executive operations ~1 at 6, ~3 at 12. Simple object recognition ~750 ms at 6, ~450 ms adult. Conflict resolution ~2000 ms at 6, ~750 ms adult.
limits: Reported without sample sizes in the summary. Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting 'capacity' (how much held) from 'control' (resisting conflict). The LLM executive-function work (a25) tests exactly that split.

source: Commons, Model of Hierarchical Complexity (via Wikipedia neo-Piagetian page)
finding: Commons proposes 16 orders of hierarchical complexity. Each order coordinates the actions of the order below.
numbers: About 20% of people perform at the systematic stage (order 11) without support. About 1.5% perform above it.
limits: Contested measure; percentages come from the model's own authors via a secondary page.
agent_relevance: Gives a ladder of complexity that could grade tasks for an agent. Weak independent validation.

source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998) Processing capacity defined by relational complexity
finding: Capacity is best measured by the number of related dimensions processed in parallel, not by item count. There is a soft limit at one quaternary relation (four arguments). More complex concepts must be segmented (serial) or chunked (collapsed), at the cost of losing access to some relations.
numbers: Unary to quaternary levels. Proportion a/b=c/d and the balance scale are quaternary. Transitivity and class inclusion are ternary; children under 5 fail when two binary relations must be integrated but succeed on one at a time. Goswami analogy mapping: 4-year-olds 86%, 3-year-olds 70%; binary-chunking baseline 67%. Fractions mapping: 4y 87%, 3y 54%.
quote: soft limit corresponding to the parallel processing of one quaternary relation
limits: A review plus a neural-net argument, not a single experiment. Authors note some tasks can be solved by binary shortcuts, so success does not prove ternary processing.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete, countable difficulty measure (arity of relation needed). We could tag task steps by arity and split any step above 4 before sending it to the model.

source: Halford et al. (1998) re-reading of A-not-B, false belief and appearance-reality
finding: The theory re-explains classic Piagetian failures as capacity limits. A-not-B means the child treats hiding place as a constant, not a variable (unary). False belief needs a ternary relation (event, actual place, believed place).
numbers: A-not-B worsens with delay and more for younger children (Wellman et al. 1986). Class inclusion difficulty before ~5y 'not fully explained'. Balance scale difficult under about 11y; adults rarely use cross-product rule without instruction (Siegler 1981; Surber & Gzesh 1984).
limits: Post hoc mapping: the arity assigned to each task is chosen by the theorists, which risks fitting after the fact.
agent_relevance: Suggests failure on multi-variable steps is a binding limit, not missing knowledge. Same pattern appears when LLMs fail relational binding in long contexts.

source: Halford et al. (1998) analysis of the balance scale
finding: The balance scale needs the quaternary relation balance-state(Wl,Dl,Wr,Dr). It can be solved by segmenting: compute moment on each side (two ternary steps), then compare (binary). McClelland's three-layer net learns it but lacks omnidirectional access to the relation.
numbers: Siegler 1981: most under 11y use lower-rank rules.
limits: Opinionated review. Does not give new data on the balance scale.
agent_relevance: Concrete example of decomposing a quaternary problem into serial ternary and binary steps, which is what a stepwise scaffold does.

source: Baillargeon, Spelke & Wasserman (1985) Object permanence in five-month-old infants (as described by the 1987 and 2000 papers)
finding: 5.5-month-olds were habituated to a screen rotating 180 degrees like a drawbridge. A box was then placed behind it. They looked longer when the screen passed through the box's space (impossible) than when it stopped at the box (possible). This was read as object permanence and solidity knowledge well before Piaget's 9 months.
numbers: Piaget (1954) put the age at about 9 months. The 1985 paper's own PDF could not be downloaded; no 1985 numbers recorded.
limits: Paper itself not opened; description comes from two later papers that open with it. Looking time is an indirect measure.
agent_relevance: Origin of the violation-of-expectation method now used to test AI physical-reasoning models.

source: Baillargeon (1987) Object permanence in 3.5- and 4.5-month-old infants
finding: Extended the drawbridge result to younger infants. 4.5-month-olds, and 3.5-month-olds who habituated fast, looked longer at the impossible event. Slow habituators did not show the effect.
numbers: Exp 1 (4.5m, N=24, ages 4m2d to 5m2d): impossible M=29.2s (SD 20.6) vs possible M=17.7s (SD 13.1), F(1,126)=14.48, p<.001; no-box control ~15-16s each. Exp 2 (3.5m, 40 tested, 12 failed to reach habituation in 9 trials): fast habituators impossible M=23.78 vs possible 14.68, F(1,189)=7.38, p<.01; slow habituators 23.45 vs 27.68, no difference.
quote: call into serious question Piaget's (1954) claims about the age at which object permanence emerges
limits: The effect depends on habituation speed, a post hoc split. Looking-time differences can come from novelty or familiarity, which is the later critique.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the same stimulus shows competence only in a subgroup. A lesson on post hoc subgroup splits when reading benchmark results.

source: Bogartz, Shinskey & Schilling (2000) Object permanence in five-and-a-half-month-old infants?
finding: Re-tested the rotating-screen design with an Event Set by Event Set design. Infants' looking times followed familiarity or novelty relations to the habituation event, not possibility of the event. So the original result need not show permanence or solidity knowledge.
numbers: Exp 1: 36 infants aged 5.5 months, 3 habituation groups of 12; a group-level test F(2,33)=3.067, p=.06. Exp 2: 52 infants, 3 vs 7 familiarisation trials; trial-number contrast F(1,48)=26.99. After 3 trials infants looked longer at the familiar rotation; after 7 trials to the 120-degree event they looked longer at the novel 180-degree event, F(1,48)=8.15.
limits: Small samples. Shows an alternative account, not that infants lack the knowledge. Other labs have argued back.
agent_relevance: Same stimulus, opposite looking direction by training length. A surprise signal in a model also needs controls for familiarity and prompt exposure.

source: Clearfield, Dineva, Smith, Diedrich & Thelen (2009) Cue salience and infant perseverative reaching
finding: Dynamic Field Theory explains the A-not-B error without a missing object concept. Reaching depends on competition between a memory of past reaches and the strength of the new cue. A stronger B cue made 9-month-olds stop perseverating.
numbers: 108 nine-month-olds (54 male, 54 female), 2 delays (0 s, 3 s) x 3 cue strengths, 18 per cell; 6 A trials then 2 B trials. Cue effect F(2,102)=7.69, p<.001; delay x cue F(2,102)=3.38, p<.05. A-trial accuracy 90% (no delay), 82% (3 s delay). Simulations: cue strength 4-17, 300 runs per condition.
limits: Cells of 18; the physical cue scale is not mapped to the model's scale.
agent_relevance: A rival to stage theory: behaviour is a dynamic state, not a stage. A stage measured once may flip with cue salience in the prompt.

source: Schapiro & McClelland (2009) A connectionist model of a continuous developmental transition in the balance scale task
finding: Siegler said children use one of four rules on the balance scale (I weight only, II adds distance when weights tie, III guessing when cues conflict, IV torque). A back-propagation network reproduces the Rule I to Rule II shift but gradually, and matches children's data better than abrupt rule switching.
numbers: Child data from Jansen & van der Maas: 314 children aged 6-10; catastrophe flags: hysteresis 7 (2.23%), sudden jump 26 (8.28%), Maxwell convention 11 (3.50%). Model: 1680 test sessions from 30 networks, chi2(5,N=1680)=28.64, p<.0001 vs child pattern.
limits: Model covers the I to II transition only. Network is trained on a fixed environment unlike children's uneven experience.
agent_relevance: Apparent stage jumps can arise from smooth learning. Be careful reading step-changes in model capability as stage changes.

source: McClelland (1989, 1995) balance-scale network (as described in Halford et al. 1998 and Schapiro & McClelland 2009)
finding: The first connectionist model of a Piagetian task. A three-layer net trained on weight and distance inputs shows Rule-I-like, then Rule-II-like, then Rule-III-like behaviour. It did not reach Rule IV without extra bias.
numbers: Rule IV 'seen only in a minority of adolescents and adults' (Siegler & Chen 2002). Original 1989 chapter not opened.
limits: Second-hand description. Fit to children is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Stage-like behaviour can come from gradient learning, not explicit rules. LLM 'stages' across scale may be smooth too.

source: Hughes (1975) policeman doll study and Borke (1975) Grover study (via Wikipedia three mountains page)
finding: Piaget and Inhelder's three mountains task said children under about 7 are egocentric. When the scene was redesigned as a hide-from-the-policeman game, most 3.5- to 5-year-olds succeeded.
numbers: Piaget task: 10 photos to choose from; age 4 picks own view, age 6 aware of others, 7-8 consistent. Hughes: 90% correct for ages 3.5-5. With extra walls and policeman dolls, 90% of 4-year-olds still passed. Borke: children as young as 3 did well with Grover.
limits: Page gives no N and no 1956 reference. Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: task framing moved the stage by 2-3 years. LLMs show the same framing sensitivity.

source: Conservation research: Piaget task, Rose & Blank (1974), McGarrigle & Donaldson (1974) (via Wikipedia)
finding: Most children fail number conservation at 4-5 and pass at 6-8; volume conservation comes around 11. Repeating the question pushes young children to change answers. When a naughty teddy made the change by accident, four-year-olds showed conservation.
numbers: Number conservation passed by most at 6-8. Volume ~11. Rose & Blank, Child Development 45(2):499-502, 1974: asking the same question twice made young children change their answer. McGarrigle & Donaldson: four-year-olds succeeded with the teddy.
limits: Page gives no N or percentages. Conservation shows decalage (different ages per quantity).
agent_relevance: A repeated question implies the first answer was wrong, a known cause of answer flips. Parallels LLM sycophancy to follow-up questions.

source: Water-level, cross-cultural, aging and balance-scale age data (Wikipedia Piaget page)
finding: Taller-beaker errors fade by about 7 to 8 years in Western samples. Non-literate groups gave more taller-means-more answers until the procedure was adapted. Older adults show a nonlinear decline on the water-level task.
numbers: Balance scale ages: 3-5y no grasp; 7y balance equal weights regardless of location; 10y consider location by trial and error; 13-14y some use weight-distance rule. Most under 12 cannot isolate pendulum variables.
limits: Summary page, no N. Formal operations are reached by fewer people than Piaget assumed.
agent_relevance: Stage attainment depends on culture, schooling and procedure. No single age of capability for an agent either.

source: Li et al. (2024/2025) CoreCognition: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
finding: A 1,503-item benchmark of 12 Piagetian core concepts, with 230 multimodal models. Models do better on high-level abilities than on sensorimotor ones. Object permanence is the weakest, and larger models show more shortcut-taking.
numbers: 12 concepts, 230 models (25 proprietary, 205 open), 11 prompts each. Permanence accuracy: human 88.10, InternVL3-78B 64.37, Gemini-1.5-Pro 59.56, GPT-4o 52.86, Qwen2.5-VL-72B 43.38, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 32.43. Mean: GPT-o1 74.91, GPT-4o 69.25, Qwen2.5-VL-72B 68.29, human 86.98. Reasoning models: no gain on 10 of 12 abilities; Perspective Taking worse (P=0.0037). A cognitive-instruction prompt gave +6%.
limits: Multimodal and VQA format adds language and counting confounds. Some table values missing in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: LLM skill growth is inverted relative to child development: low-level skills lag high-level ones. A stage ladder is the wrong model for LLM skill growth.

source: Li et al. (2024) Concept Hacking test inside CoreCognition
finding: A controlled test inverts the correct label by changing causal features. Few models do as well on flipped items as on originals, so many answers use shortcuts.
numbers: 45 paired samples. Perspective Taking declines as models grow, which the authors call a persistent egocentric bias.
limits: Small paired set. Labour-intensive and not scaled.
agent_relevance: Use matched paired items with flipped answers when we test an agent, to separate understanding from pattern priors.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) CogLM: Piaget-based cognitive ability evaluation for language models
finding: CogLM gives 1,220 multiple-choice items over 10 Piagetian abilities, mapped to a human age scale from 141 valid human respondents. GPT-4 scores at about the 20-year-old level, GPT-3.5 at 16, Llama-2-chat-70B at 14, OPT-6.7B at 6.5.
numbers: Stage items: S1 150, S2 200, S3 310, S4 560. Humans: 207 aged 6-20, 141 valid; age-score Spearman 0.7169, Pearson 0.7362. Calibrated accuracy: OPT-6.7B 15.5%, Llama-2-chat-70B 54.6%, GPT-3.5 64.0%, GPT-4 84.7%, adult human 93.7%. GPT-4 planning 59.4% vs human 95.6%. CoT 64.3 and self-consistency 64.4 vs 64.0 baseline.
limits: Age map extrapolates beyond 20 from a 6-20 sample. Multiple choice only. Table 9 shows base and chat Llama-2-70B identical, which conflicts with the claim that chat is far better.
agent_relevance: Scaling lifts all stages, and CoT adds almost nothing on these items. Planning is the largest gap, which supports a plan-checking operator.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) CogLM ability-erasure and Chain-of-Cognition
finding: Prompting to suppress early abilities lowered later ones, with constancy most foundational. Reasoning written by GPT-3.5 raised Llama-2-chat-7B from 31.0 to 38.1 average.
numbers: Erasure lowered GPT-3.5 on GSM8K and StrategyQA. Chain-of-Cognition +7.1 points on Llama-2-chat-7B.
limits: Erasure by prompt is a weak manipulation. Small downstream sets.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that guiding a small model with a stronger model's scaffolded reasoning helps. Not tested on frontier models.

source: Su et al. (2024) Vision Language Models Know Law of Conservation without Understanding More-or-Less (ConserveBench)
finding: On 365 conservation items, vision-language models pass transformation tasks (reversibility) but fail single-image quantity tasks. This is a dissociation between reversibility and more-or-less.
numbers: 5 VLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4-mini, CogVLM2, BLIP2). Overall at or below 38%. GPT-4o: 97.44% on transformational tasks, 31.22% on non-transformational, 22.11% on number. GPT-4o chose the opposite of the human length-equals-number bias.
limits: Five models, per-model detail only for GPT-4o. The dense-equals-more explanation is untested. Human data planned, not collected.
agent_relevance: Passing the textbook task does not mean the concept is held. Test both the transformed and static versions.

source: ConservationBench (2026): 112 VLMs on number, length, volume, size conservation
finding: Most vision-language models fail Piagetian conservation once controls are added. They answer conserve by default, so they pass conserving items and fail non-conserving ones.
numbers: 112 VLMs 1B-76B; 192 conservation + 192 non-conserving videos; 23,040 trials. Human: conserve 98.55, non-conserve 98.15. gemini-2.5-pro 94.33/43.88; gpt-5 91.48/35.82; claude-sonnet-4-5 75.43/45.39. 82 of 112 models (73.2%) strict accuracy under 10%. Conserve vs non-conserve accuracy r=-0.510. Blank images: Conserve answered 85.7%. Text-only: 73.7%. Size vs conservation accuracy R2=0.019. CoT worse than other prompts on number/length (p<.001).
limits: Behavioural only; four properties; controlled lab clips; only 3 of 112 above chance on strict score.
agent_relevance: High accuracy came from a prior, not perception. Always include the not-conserved twin of each item when grading an agent.

source: Gong et al. (2023) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: ChatGPT shows an n-back capacity limit of about 3, close to human estimates. Noise cut capacity, spatial capacity was lower than verbal, and chain-of-thought helped spatial tasks.
numbers: Verbal n-back d' falls to about 1 at n=3 for GPT-3.5. 50 blocks of 24 trials per n. GPT-3.5 Kruskal-Wallis H=58.54, p=1.94e-13; GPT-4 H=52.51 and d' stayed above 1 at n=1-3. Open 6-13B models: no effect of n, d' not above 1 (p .126-.99).
limits: GPT-4 tested only to n=3; d'=1 threshold chosen by authors; letter X stimuli only.
agent_relevance: Neo-Piagetian tie: capacity limits appear in LLMs, but the limit moves with model quality. Supports keeping per-step load low.

source: Strong Memory, Weak Control (2025): executive functioning in LLMs
finding: Six open models (Gemma2, Llama3.1, Qwen2; 7B-72B) beat human norms on span tasks but fall below humans on attention control and flexibility. Capacity is not the bottleneck; control is.
numbers: Operation span 0.92-0.99 vs human 0.53. Reading span 0.66-0.98 vs 0.48. 3-back 0.67-0.85 vs 0.75. WCST 0.29-0.53 vs 0.77. Flanker incongruent 0.40-0.60 vs 0.93-0.96. Reasoning raised flanker: Llama-3.1-8B 0.471 to 0.910; no gain on WCST. Parameters vs span r=0.82, p<0.05. 30 prompt variants per task.
limits: Open-weight models only; human baselines come from other studies; reasoning traces are token-heavy.
agent_relevance: Mirror image of neo-Piagetian growth by capacity: LLMs have plenty of capacity but weak control. A scaffold should add control (checks, set switching), not memory.

source: Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory (2025), search-result level only
finding: A search summary says the paper argues LLMs lack core features of human working memory and that context windows are an engineering workaround.
numbers: No numbers recorded; the page was not opened.
limits: Not read. Treat as a pointer only.
agent_relevance: Counter-view to Gong et al. 2023; read before citing.

source: Demetriou et al. (Nov 2025 preprint) linking LLM cognition to developmental theory (search result only)
finding: Per a search summary, it claims LLMs reach around formal-operations level on some tasks and that working memory and rehearsal quality drive relational processing.
numbers: No numbers; the page returned 403 and was not opened.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed, not read.
agent_relevance: Closest neo-Piagetian LLM paper found. Needs reading in angle B or C.

source: Siegler (1976) Three aspects of cognitive development, and Siegler & Chen (2002) (as described in Schapiro & McClelland 2009)
finding: Siegler used six balance-scale item types (balance, weight, distance, conflict-weight, conflict-distance, conflict-balance) and classified children by rule. Rule IV, the torque rule, appears only in a minority of adolescents and adults.
numbers: Rules I to IV as above. Jansen & van der Maas tested 314 children aged 6-10 on 40 items.
limits: Siegler's 1976 paper not opened. Later work (Boom et al.; van der Maas) disputes strict rule classification.
agent_relevance: Rule assessment is a template for probing which strategy an LLM uses by designing items where rules disagree.

source: Overall boundary-condition pattern across the founding tasks
finding: Across tasks, earlier success appears whenever the demand is lowered: teddy for conservation, policeman for perspective taking, looking for reaching. Later work asks whether the early success reflects the concept or a bias.
numbers: Examples: conservation 6-8y vs teddy 4y; mountains 7-8y vs policeman 90% at 3.5-5y; object permanence 9 months vs 3.5-5.5 months by looking.
limits: Synthesis across secondary sources and two primary papers.
agent_relevance: Report capability only with a matched pair of low- and high-demand task versions.
